title: Count and Say
description: Brute force to optimized: repeated string concatenation versus a growable buffer versus exploiting the bounded run length.

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement

Problem Summary: The count and say sequence is a sequence of strings where term 1 is "1", and every following term is built by reading the previous term aloud, digit run by digit run, and writing down how many of each digit appear consecutively followed by that digit itself. Given n, return the nth term of this sequence.

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem

The count and say sequence is a sequence of strings where term 1 is "1", and every following term is built by reading the previous term aloud, digit run by digit run, and writing down how many of each digit appear consecutively followed by that digit itself. Given n, return the nth term of this sequence.

blocks.title: Analogy: Describing a Row of Repeated Digits Out Loud
blocks.text: Imagine reading a row of digits aloud the way a person naturally would: instead of naming every digit one at a time, group the identical neighbors together and say how many of them there are, followed by which digit it is, for example "two 1s, one 2" instead of "1, 1, 2".

blocks.caption: Each term is generated by describing the runs of digits in the previous term

blocks.text: Edge case: n = 1
The first term is defined directly as the base case "1". There is nothing to describe yet, so no group reading step happens at all.
5. How Should We Think?

The run-scanning logic itself, find consecutive identical digits and count them, is the obvious part. It is worth pausing on the part that small examples hide entirely: how the next term's string actually gets assembled.

blocks.title: How Should We Think?
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Finding a run of identical digits and counting its length is a straightforward single pass, nothing about that logic is genuinely difficult or hides any trap.

Observation 2: Since strings are immutable in most languages, every "+" or "+=" concatenation silently allocates a brand new string and copies everything built so far into it, a cost that is invisible for a short string but very much not invisible as terms grow.

Observation 3: Count-and-say term lengths grow roughly geometrically from one term to the next, so the very last term, by far the longest, ends up dominating the total work, and building an L-length string through repeated concatenation costs proportional to L squared, not L.

Observation 4: Swapping that immutable concatenation for a mutable, growable buffer, appended to in place and converted to a string only once at the very end, turns the same single scanning pass into a genuinely linear construction too.

That distinction, a scan that is already linear versus a construction step that quietly is not, is exactly what separates a solution that looks fine on short terms from one that stays fast as terms grow long.
6. Brute Force Solution

Start from term 1 and build every following term up through term n, one at a time. For each term, scan it left to right, find each run of identical digits, and grow the next term's string with the plus operator every time a run is described.
Step by step algorithm

items: Start with term equal to "1".
Repeat n minus 1 times: scan the current term to find runs of identical consecutive digits.
For each run, append its length and its digit onto a new string using the plus operator.
Replace the current term with this newly built string and move to the next iteration.

blocks.caption: Brute force: rebuild the next term with repeated plus-equals concatenation

codes.python:
def count_and_say(n):
    term = "1"                                              # term 1 is always the string "1"
    for _ in range(n - 1):                                   # build term 2, then 3, all the way through term n
        next_term = ""                                        # start this term's string from scratch
        i = 0
        while i < len(term):
            digit = term[i]
            count = 1
            while i + count < len(term) and term[i + count] == digit:
                count += 1                                        # extend the run while the same digit repeats
            next_term += str(count) + digit                       # re-creates a brand new string on every append
            i += count
        term = next_term
    return term


if __name__ == "__main__":
    n = 5
    print(count_and_say(n))

7. Analyze the Brute Force
This is correct, since every run of identical digits is found and described in order, exactly matching the sequence's own definition.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(L squared) for building the final term of length L, since immutable string concatenation copies the whole string built so far on every single append.
Space: O(L), for the final term, though the repeated copying above uses far more transient memory than that in practice.

Limitation: term lengths grow roughly geometrically from one term to the next, so the very last term dominates the total work, and building that one term through repeated concatenation is quadratic in its own length instead of linear.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why repeated concatenation works but is wasteful: the plus operator allocates a brand new string and copies everything built so far into it, on every single append, even though nothing about the already-built portion has changed.

What the run-scanning logic itself actually needs: to visit each character of the current term exactly once, which is already a linear pass with no hidden cost of its own.

Can the construction step be made to match that same linear cost: yes, a mutable, growable buffer accepts each new piece in place, without re-copying anything already stored in it.

When does the buffer actually become a plain string: only once, after the entire scan finishes, converting the whole buffer to a string in a single final operation.

The core idea: keep the same run scanning logic unchanged, but collect each run's count and digit into a growable buffer instead of concatenating with the plus operator, and convert that buffer to the final term string only once.

The bottleneck is the plus operator itself: every single append allocates a brand new string and copies everything built so far into it. Swapping that out for a mutable, growable buffer, a list joined once at the end in Python, a StringBuilder in Java, or a reserved string with in place appends in C++, lets each term be built in time proportional to its own length instead of the square of its length.
9. Optimized Solution

Keep the same run scanning logic, but collect each run's count and digit into a growable buffer instead of concatenating with the plus operator, and only convert that buffer into the final term string once, after the whole scan finishes.
Dry run for building term 5 from term 4 = "1211"

blocks.caption: Optimized: collect each run into a buffer, convert to a string only once at the end

codes.python:
def count_and_say(n):
    term = "1"
    for _ in range(n - 1):
        parts = []                                            # collect pieces once, join only at the very end
        i = 0
        while i < len(term):
            digit = term[i]
            count = 1
            while i + count < len(term) and term[i + count] == digit:
                count += 1
            parts.append(str(count))
            parts.append(digit)
            i += count
        term = ''.join(parts)                                  # a single allocation for the whole new term
    return term


if __name__ == "__main__":
    n = 5
    print(count_and_say(n))

blocks.text: Why This Works

This works because a growable buffer, unlike an immutable string, can accept new content in place, without re-copying everything already stored in it; the total work across every append is therefore proportional to the final length once, not to that length squared. Converting the buffer to a plain string happens exactly once, after the scan finishes, so that single conversion cost is also only ever paid once per term, not once per append.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What Happens","Result"],"rows":[["Each run is found during the scan","Its count and digit are appended directly into the growable buffer","No existing content in the buffer is ever re-copied to make room for the new piece"],["The scan of the current term finishes","The buffer is converted into a plain string exactly once","The next term is produced with a single final conversion instead of one allocation per append"]]}

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(L), where L is the length of the final term, since the buffer grows in place instead of being recopied on every append.
Space: O(L), for the buffer and the resulting term.
10. Further Optimization: Exploiting the Bounded Run Length

A property of this exact sequence is that a run of the same digit can never be longer than 3. If a digit ever repeated 4 or more times, the term that produced that run would itself have needed to describe a count of 4 or more, which would introduce a new digit into that earlier term and break the run apart one step sooner, so runs of 4 or more never actually occur. Since count is always guaranteed to be 1, 2, or 3, it can be converted to its digit character directly with simple arithmetic instead of calling a general purpose integer to string function.

codes.python:
def count_and_say(n):
    term = "1"
    for _ in range(n - 1):
        parts = []
        i = 0
        while i < len(term):
            digit = term[i]
            count = 1
            while i + count < len(term) and term[i + count] == digit:
                count += 1                                          # count is guaranteed to be 1, 2, or 3, never more
            parts.append(chr(ord('0') + count))                      # direct single character arithmetic, no str() call
            parts.append(digit)
            i += count
        term = ''.join(parts)
    return term


if __name__ == "__main__":
    n = 5
    print(count_and_say(n))

blocks.text: Code walkthrough

items: The run-scanning logic is completely unchanged from the previous round, only how a run's count gets turned into a character is different.

Since count is mathematically guaranteed to be 1, 2, or 3 in this specific sequence, adding it directly to the character 0 produces the correct digit character without ever calling a general string-conversion function.
This removes a small but real constant-factor cost, a full conversion routine, per group, replacing it with a single character addition.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(L), the same asymptotic bound as the previous round, now with a cheaper constant per group since no general purpose conversion function is called.
Space: O(L), unchanged.

blocks.text: 12. Key Takeaways

This is a simulation and string building problem whose real trap is not the run length counting logic itself, which is straightforward, but how the next term's string gets assembled, since naive concatenation quietly turns an otherwise linear idea into a quadratic one.
Common Mistakes

items: Building each term with repeated string concatenation, which is correct but far slower than it needs to be as terms grow longer.
Off by one errors in the inner run counting loop, especially at the very last character of a term.
Confusing "n" (which term to return) with the length of that term, they are unrelated quantities.

blocks.text: Interview Tips

Mention the bounded run length property, never more than 3, if asked to optimize further, it shows a deeper understanding of why this specific sequence behaves the way it does; also point out early that this problem has no closed form shortcut, term n truly depends on the exact content of term n minus 1, so every earlier term must be materialized in turn.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text:
If the interviewer says "why is your solution slow for large n", think: immutable string concatenation recopies the whole string on every append, swap in a growable buffer.
If the interviewer says "can you optimize further", think: the bounded run length, never more than 3, allows direct character arithmetic instead of a general conversion call.
If the interviewer says "can you skip directly to term n", think: no, this sequence has no closed form, every earlier term must genuinely be built in turn.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: Why does immutable string concatenation turn an otherwise linear construction into a quadratic one?
Can you prove more rigorously why a run in this sequence can never exceed length 3?
How would you adapt this simulation to run entirely in place, reusing the same buffer across terms instead of allocating a new one each time?
How would the approach change if you needed to return every term from 1 to n, not just the nth one?
How would you estimate the length of term n without actually constructing every earlier term?

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: Any problem building a string through many small pieces, where immutable concatenation is a common but easy to miss performance trap.
Zigzag Conversion, which shares this same lesson, collecting pieces into per-row buffers instead of repeatedly reallocating strings.
Run length encoding and decoding problems in general, which reuse this exact run-scanning technique in both directions.
Problems with a mathematically provable bound on some intermediate quantity, like this sequence's run length, which can unlock a cheaper constant-factor implementation once identified.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: Brute force: O(L squared) time due to repeated string concatenation, O(L) space, where L is the length of the final term. Optimized: O(L) time using a growable buffer, O(L) space. Further optimized: O(L) time with a cheaper per-group constant from direct character arithmetic, O(L) space.
13. Final Summary

items: Pattern: run length encoding simulation, where the real difficulty is not the run-scanning logic but the hidden cost of how the next term's string gets assembled.

Core Idea: immutable string concatenation silently recopies everything built so far on every append, so collecting pieces into a growable buffer and converting to a string only once turns a quadratic construction into a linear one.
Time: O(L squared) for the brute force, O(L) for both the optimized and further optimized versions, where L is the length of the final term.
Space: O(L) for all three versions.
Most Important Observation: a scan that is already linear can still hide a quadratic cost in how its output gets assembled, if that assembly uses immutable concatenation.
Interview Difficulty: easy to write a correct brute force; recognizing the hidden concatenation cost, and separately, proving the bounded run length property, is what shows real understanding.
One line memory trick: collect pieces in a growable buffer, join once at the end, never concatenate immutable strings in a loop.
